description: Somos a equipe Space Doctor, com Paulo e Alexandre, medalhistas em Astronomia! Vamos criar um app gamificado de saúde para astronautas. Unimos paixão pelo espaço, tecnologias e medicina. Buscamos parceiros criativos com habilidades em programação para codificar essa missão. Venha construir o melhor médico virtual para salvar vidas no espaço!

details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Advanced Space Life Supporter (ASLS) is a hub that brings a 3D training game and a decision-support app together in one place. It is built for crews far from Earth, where the flight surgeon can be up to 24 minutes away. When the flight surgeon is out of reach, ASLS guides astronauts to the best health decision. It never diagnoses. The hub has three entries:

  • Play the Game (3D training): inside a spacecraft cabin, the player takes the role of the crew medical officer. They measure blood pressure, heart rate, SpO2 and temperature, listen to the heart and lungs with a guided stethoscope, run triage, choose a treatment and practice a cardiac-arrest response in microgravity with an AED, CPR and the LUCAS 3 device. Each exam earns XP and explains why it matters.
  • Space Doc (decision-support app): a live health dashboard with 13 screens. It turns every reading into a green, yellow or red alert and follows a 3-layer protocol that runs at the same time: an autonomous layer for what cannot wait, an assisted layer that guides each dose step by step, and a handoff layer that builds a 10-line summary for the flight surgeon. With no link to Earth, it keeps working and queues data until the next communication window.
  • Strategic Planning & Hardware: explains how the system would work on board, from wireless sensors to power use.

Real data drive the experience. NASA DONKI space-weather alerts and NOAA proton flux become radiation-risk warnings, and the live ISS position shows the crew’s environment. NASA Human Research Program hazards and CSA experiments (Radi-N2, Vascular, TBone, MARROW, Wayfinding, Microflow) shape each health indicator.

What benefits does it have?
Most crew medical officers are not physicians. ASLS helps them in two ways: the game trains them before the mission, and the app supports them during it. It flags warning signs early, guides safe action step by step, keeps an auditable record of every decision and works without a link to Earth. Final medical decisions stay with the flight surgeon whenever contact is possible.

What is the intended impact?
In space, it supports long missions to the Moon and Mars, where crews must act on their own between communication windows. On Earth, the same idea can guide anyone far from a hospital, such as people in remote villages, on ships, in mines or in ambulances. As an educational game, it also teaches young people how the human body reacts to space.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?
HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D scenes and the Web Audio API for synthesized heart, lung and bowel sounds. We used the NASA DONKI API, NOAA SWPC data and the wheretheiss.at ISS API, with Python and edge-tts for the English narration and FFmpeg for the video. It is a static site that runs in any browser, on phone, tablet or computer, with no installation. AI tools (Claude) helped write code, text and audio, and the team reviewed and tested everything.

How is your project creative?
It joins a training game and a real-use app in one hub, so learning and doing happen in the same place. It turns space weather into a health alert, lets players hear synthesized heart and lung sounds, and simulates the real communication delay with Earth. It also tells a story: a crew on day 187 on the way to Mars, where the player must care for a crewmate until help from Earth arrives.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Communication delay and offline work: the protocol changes by environment (low Earth orbit, Moon, Mars).
  • Safety: the system guides decisions but never diagnoses. Every drug release needs confirmation and is logged for the flight surgeon to review.
  • Microgravity: CPR methods and airway guidance follow published evidence on resuscitation in microgravity.
  • Accessibility: the layout is responsive, with English captions, narration and text.
  • Privacy: no personal data is collected.
  • Responsible design: educational use only, not medical advice.
